title: Disaster Recovery
subtitle: The four cloud DR spectrum tiers (Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, Multi-Site Active-Active) and chaos validation.
keyTakeaways: Cloud Disaster Recovery spans four progressive patterns, Backup & Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active-Active, trading recurring infrastructure cost against RPO/RTO speed.
In a Pilot Light architecture, only the stateful data core (database replicas) runs continuously in the DR region while stateless compute stays at 0 instances until scaled up during an incident.

An untested DR plan is a fiction: immutable off-account backups (to survive ransomware) and automated Chaos Engineering drills (DiRT / GameDays) are mandatory to prevent cloud capacity-limit surprises during real outages.

sections.heading: The Four Cloud Disaster Recovery Tiers
sections.body: Selecting a Disaster Recovery (DR) strategy requires balancing the probability and hourly cost of a catastrophic regional outage against the 24/7 run-rate of standby cloud resources.
bullets: 1. Backup & Restore (RPO: Hours, RTO: 2-24 Hours): Cross-region S3 snapshots + Terraform/IaC templates. Zero idle compute cost, but slow restoration and vulnerable to cloud API throttling when provisioning hundreds of nodes from scratch.

2. Pilot Light (RPO: Seconds, RTO: 15-45 Minutes): The 'pilot flame' (cross-region async DB replica and container registries) is always running and synced, while stateless app ASGs sit at 0 capacity and boot only on failover.

3. Warm Standby (RPO: Seconds, RTO: 5-15 Minutes): A scaled-down (e.g., 15-25% capacity) but fully functional copy of the entire stack runs in the DR region, continuously handling synthetic traffic and ready to scale horizontally.
4. Multi-Site Active-Active (RPO: 0-Seconds, RTO: Near-Zero): Full production capacity runs across multiple regions simultaneously, shifting traffic via global load balancers in seconds.

sections.heading: Ransomware Air-Gapping, Failback Hazards, and Chaos GameDays
sections.body: Real-world disasters include not only natural disasters and cloud outages, but also compromised IAM credentials, accidental `terraform destroy` runs, and supply-chain ransomware.
bullets: Air-Gapped Immutable Backups (AWS Vault Lock / WORM): Replicate backups to an isolated 'Security Vault' AWS/GCP account with Object Lock (Write-Once-Read-Many) so even a compromised root credential in the production account cannot delete backups.

Cloud Iceberg / Capacity Exhaustion Risk: In Pilot Light and Warm Standby, if an entire cloud region goes down, thousands of companies simultaneously request EC2 instances in the neighboring DR region, often hitting `InsufficientInstanceCapacity` errors unless On-Demand Capacity Reservations are held.

The Failback Trap: Failing *back* to the original primary region after it recovers is often riskier than the initial failover because data written to the DR region during the outage must be reverse-replicated and reconciled before switching traffic back.

tradeOffs.pros: Keeps database RPO within seconds while paying almost zero for idle stateless compute instances.
tradeOffs.cons: Risk of cloud capacity exhaustion when scaling compute from 0 to 100% during a mass regional event; 30-minute RTO.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core business applications that cannot lose data (low RPO) but can tolerate 20-30 minutes of downtime.

tradeOffs.pros: Continuously validates the full application stack via synthetic probes; much faster RTO (5-15m).
tradeOffs.cons: Incurs 20-30% extra baseline compute, load balancer, and NAT gateway costs 24/7.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Customer-facing e-commerce, API platforms, and SaaS systems with <15 minute RTO commitments.

interviewTip: Mention the 'Failback Problem' in interviews: anyone can draw an arrow flipping DNS to Region B, but Staff candidates explain how mutations accumulated in Region B during the 3-hour outage are safely replicated back to Region A before restoring normal operations.
